summaryCard: Bengal sharecroppers refused to hand landlords half their harvest, demanding two-thirds instead, and for a time took control of the threshing floor from Dinajpur to the Sundarbans.
fullEntry: Under Bengal's sharecropping system, bargadars (sharecroppers) who worked land owned by jotedars (landholders) were required to hand over half their harvest as rent. In 1938-40, the Bengal Land Revenue Commission (the Floud Commission) recommended reducing that share to one-third, but the Bengal government did not act on it. In September 1946, the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS), the peasant wing of the then-undivided Communist Party of India, called for a mass movement to enforce the tebhaga (three-shares) demand from the coming aman harvest: 'adhi noy, tebhaga chai' (we want two-thirds, not half). The movement is generally traced to the Thakurgaon subdivision of Dinajpur, where sharecroppers began carrying harvested paddy to their own threshing floors rather than the landlord's godown, denying jotedars the ability to control the division. The tactic spread rapidly; landlords in some areas fled and the Kisan Sabha effectively controlled the countryside. Reports from the period describe over a thousand arrests between September and December 1946 alone. In early 1947, Bengal's Suhrawardy government introduced the State Acquisition and Tenancy Bill and the Bengal Bargadars (Provisional) Bill to legislate something close to the tebhaga demand, but Partition intervened before either could be enacted. After Partition, the movement continued on both sides of the new border under very different conditions -- see the linked Nachole uprising for its continuation in East Bengal (Pakistan). Some historians describe the movement's immediate demands as largely unmet outside particular pockets, since legislative follow-through was overtaken by Partition; others emphasize the durable organizing legacy it left for later land-reform politics in West Bengal.

summaryCard: In East Pakistan, Santal peasants and sharecroppers around Nachole carried the tebhaga demand forward until a police crackdown in January 1950 crushed the uprising and its leader, Ila Mitra, was arrested and tortured.
fullEntry: After Partition split Bengal, the tebhaga struggle continued in East Bengal (Pakistan) under harsher conditions, concentrated around Nachole in Rajshahi district (now Chapainawabganj, Bangladesh) where the peasantry was largely Santal. Organized with Communist Party support and led locally by Ila Mitra, the movement pressed jotedars to accept the two-thirds share. On 5 January 1950, a police patrol clashed with a Santal peasant group at Kendua; accounts describe several police personnel killed. The state responded with a large deployment of police and paramilitary Ansar forces, and, by some accounts, the burning of a number of villages in the area. Ila Mitra was arrested while attempting to flee, held at Nachole police station, and -- this is well documented across multiple sources -- subjected to severe torture including sexual assault before being moved to Rajshahi Central Jail. She was convicted on charges related to the uprising and sentenced to life imprisonment; ill health from the torture led to her parole in 1954. Casualty figures for the uprising itself vary significantly by source and are not settled here -- flag this in the full site rather than picking a single number.

summaryCard: The Bengal Land Revenue Commission recommends sharecroppers keep two-thirds of the crop instead of half -- a demand the government did not act on for six years.
fullEntry: Appointed in 1938 to review Bengal's agrarian system, the Bengal Land Revenue Commission (popularly the Floud Commission) reported that sharecroppers should be treated as protected tenants and that their legally recoverable share should fall from half to one-third for the landlord, i.e. two-thirds for the cultivator. The government of the day did not implement the recommendation, but it gave the Kisan Sabha's later demand the weight of an official finding.
title: Floud Commission recommends the tebhaga share

sources.citation: The Tebhaga Movement: A Revolutionary Peasant Uprising in Bengal, PolSci Institute

summaryCard: The Kisan Sabha formally decides to launch the tebhaga struggle from the next harvest.
fullEntry: In September 1946, the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) resolved to launch a mass struggle to enforce the tebhaga demand starting with that season's aman (winter) harvest, against the backdrop of communal riots elsewhere in Bengal. The call built on an earlier, war- and famine-delayed resolution from a 1940 Kisan Sabha conference.
title: Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha calls for tebhaga

sources.citation: A Struggle for Fair Share: Recounting the Tebhaga Movement, 1946-47, Labour File

summaryCard: Sharecroppers in Dinajpur begin carrying harvested paddy to their own threshing floors instead of the landlord's godown, sparking the movement's first clashes.
fullEntry: The first direct action is generally traced to Atwari village in northwest Dinajpur, where bargadar volunteers harvested their fields and carried the grain to their own khamar rather than the jotedar's storehouse. Landlords responded with hired enforcers and police; violent clashes followed, Kisan Sabha organizers were arrested, and the movement spread outward to an estimated 19 districts of undivided Bengal.
title: Movement breaks out in Dinajpur

sources.citation: The history of the Tebhaga Movement, Dhaka Tribune

summaryCard: The Suhrawardy government introduces bills to legislate the tebhaga demand, but Partition intervenes before either becomes law.
fullEntry: In response to the movement, Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy's Bengal government introduced the State Acquisition and Tenancy Bill and the Bengal Bargadars (Provisional) Bill in early 1947, aiming to abolish the Permanent Settlement and improve sharecroppers' legal position. Neither was enacted before Partition split the province and its legislature.
title: Bargadar bills introduced, then overtaken by Partition

sources.citation: Ila Mitra: A symbol of indomitable courage, The Daily Star

summaryCard: A patrol clashes with Santal peasants; the state responds with a large police and paramilitary deployment.
fullEntry: On 5 January 1950 a police patrol in Kendua, near Nachole, clashed with a group of Santal peasants; accounts describe several police personnel killed in the confrontation. The government deployed a large force of police and Ansar paramilitary in response, and multiple villages in the area reportedly came under attack in the aftermath. Ila Mitra was arrested in the days that followed. Casualty figures on both sides vary by source.
title: Police clash at Kendua, Nachole

sources.citation: The history of the Tebhaga Movement, Dhaka Tribune

summaryCard: The tebhaga-era demand is finally partly legislated -- not in India, but in East Bengal, four years after the movement began.
fullEntry: The 1947 bills that Partition had left unenacted were reworked and reintroduced in the East Bengal Legislative Assembly. The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act became law on 16 December 1950, abolishing the zamindari-era Permanent Settlement in East Bengal and incorporating tebhaga-type sharecropping provisions.
title: East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act

summaryCard: Led the Santal and sharecropper uprising around Nachole; arrested and tortured in 1950 for it, later paroled on health grounds.
fullEntry: Born Ila Sen in Kolkata in 1925, she was selected for the 1940 Olympics as an athlete before the Games were cancelled by the war. After her 1945 marriage to Ramendra Mitra, she settled in Chapainawabganj and became a teacher and organizer among the local Santal and peasant community, who called her Rani Ma (queen mother). She led the tebhaga-era organizing that culminated in the January 1950 Nachole uprising. Arrested while fleeing after the Kendua clash, she was held at Nachole police station where she was tortured, including sexual assault -- documented consistently across the sources checked for this entry -- before being moved to Rajshahi Central Jail. Convicted on charges related to the uprising, she was sentenced to life imprisonment and paroled in 1954 due to ill health, going to Kolkata for treatment.
name: Ila Mitra
